item.title: Microsoft fixes Windows activation as admins pick through Exchange outage wreckage
item.description: Microsoft has released an out-of-band update to fix licensing and activation errors introduced by November's Windows security update. The fix is available from the Microsoft Update Catalog for Windows Server 2025, 2022, and 2019, Windows 10 22H2 ESU, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 and 2019. Windows 11 23H2 users can obtain it from the Catalog or through Windows Update's Optional updates menu. The "non-security OOB update" targets affected enterprise devices. Microsoft stated: "Certain Windows licensing and activation operations using the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) might fail with error 0x80041008 (Invalid parameter). "This primarily affects organizations using slmgr.vbs commands or automated processes to configure Key Management Service (KMS) activation, install product keys, or manage Windows licensing." Devices that are already activated will remain activated, Microsoft said. Breaking the machinery customers use to activate paid-for software is a bad look for a Patch Tuesday release . Administrators may wonder how Microsoft's updates are tested when installing one means waiting for another to repair the damage. Those same administrators may also have been fielding calls about last week's widespread Exchange Online outage, which Microsoft has partly attributed to a defect it introduced in July . On top of that, Microsoft told administrators just days ago to consider unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 " permanently vulnerable ." Exchange Online avoids that particular support deadline, but the recent outage was a reminder that handing over the servers doesn't make software defects disappear. Forget "security by obscurity." Last week's approach was more like "security by unavailability." Between getting Windows activated and keeping Exchange Online online, Microsoft gave administrators plenty to do. None of it was likely to feature in their original plans for the week. Not all the glitches introduced by November's Patch Tuesday have yet been resolved, as some customers using a Windows device to print will be aware. ®

item.title: ‘Spiraling’ Trailer: Toni Tones and Jim Iyke Star in Nigerian Psychological Thriller About an Affair That Turns Deadly
item.description: The official trailer for Spiraling , a Nigerian psychological thriller starring Toni Tones ( King of Boys, The Smart Money Woman ), Jim Iyke (Bad Comments, Merry Men 2) , Seun Ajayi ((Japa, The Smart Money Woman ) and Folu Storms (Red Circle, Baby Farm) , has been unveiled ahead of the series’ release on November 26th. Set against the backdrop of a historic election, the series follows Sade (Tones), a successful tech entrepreneur whose carefully constructed life begins to unravel after an impulsive affair sets off a chain of deception and betrayal. Spiraling Series/Instagram What begins as a private indiscretion quickly threatens Sade’s relationships, reputation and everything she has worked to build. The series explores the consequences of desire, ambition and the lengths people will go to protect their carefully constructed lives. Spiraling is created and directed by Wande Thomas and produced by Thomas and Isoken Ogiemwonyi through Urbangidi Showtime and Studio Ogiso . The four-part thriller marks another addition to KAVA’s growing catalogue of African film and television content. Spiraling launches on November 26, 2026 exclusively on streaming platform KAVA . Watch the official trailer for Spiraling below. item.title: Crook turns free trials into phishing factory, as LearnWorlds sends 13,000 fake YouTube copyright notices
item.description: LearnWorlds, a software and learning course platform, says an attacker sent 13,000 phishing emails to customers over seven days by using automated tools to open free trial accounts. The company insists its systems were not breached. Panos Siozos, Co-founder and CEO at LearnWorlds, said the miscreant created around 570 free trial accounts on the platform between November 7-14, which they used to issue fake copyright infringement notices to customers. "We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to existing customer schools or personal data held for our customers and their end users," he told The Register . According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails. "In each trial they added their own list of target addresses and rewrote the standard welcome email as a fake copyright notice," he said. "Adding those users triggered the welcome email from our sending address." The first email was sent on November 7, after which the company detected the suspicious signups and blocked the first sender on November 9, although the attacker returned to send a second wave of emails within 40 minutes. LearnWorlds removed all the trial accounts by November 10 and one paid account, which was used to launch more emails, on November 14. "In total, around 13,000 emails were sent to addresses on external recipient lists supplied by the sender," said Siozos. "The trial accounts sent 9,853 between November 7-9, and the paid account sent 3,723 on November 14. "We can’t tell how many people clicked, because the link was disguised to hide clicks. The recipient addresses were the sender’s own list." The CEO confirmed that LearnWorlds has since enhanced its bot checks and is placing holds on new accounts if their emails trigger fraud flags. "We have also examined the novel patterns the attackers used to create more advanced scoring mechanisms. We have reported the phishing website so it can be taken down. Further measures are currently being examined. "Anyone who signed in on the fake page should change their Google password and review their account’s recent security activity." The company's confirmation follows suspicions of foul play aired by users on social media. User reports included copies of the emails they received, which demanded urgent responses to fake copyright infringement claims related to YouTube content. Among the more prominent recipients of the copyright infringement email notices was Marcus Hutchins, of WannaCry fame , who claimed he received an email from the company’s official mail server. item.dc:creator: Connor Jones
item.content:encoded: LearnWorlds, a software and learning course platform, says an attacker sent 13,000 phishing emails to customers over seven days by using automated tools to open free trial accounts. The company insists its systems were not breached. Panos Siozos, Co-founder and CEO at LearnWorlds, said the miscreant created around 570 free trial accounts on the platform between November 7-14, which they used to issue fake copyright infringement notices to customers. "We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to existing customer schools or personal data held for our customers and their end users," he told The Register . According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails. "In each trial they added their own list of target addresses and rewrote the standard welcome email as a fake copyright notice," he said. "Adding those users triggered the welcome email from our sending address." The first email was sent on November 7, after which the company detected the suspicious signups and blocked the first sender on November 9, although the attacker returned to send a second wave of emails within 40 minutes. LearnWorlds removed all the trial accounts by November 10 and one paid account, which was used to launch more emails, on November 14. "In total, around 13,000 emails were sent to addresses on external recipient lists supplied by the sender," said Siozos. "The trial accounts sent 9,853 between November 7-9, and the paid account sent 3,723 on November 14. "We can’t tell how many people clicked, because the link was disguised to hide clicks. The recipient addresses were the sender’s own list." The CEO confirmed that LearnWorlds has since enhanced its bot checks and is placing holds on new accounts if their emails trigger fraud flags. "We have also examined the novel patterns the attackers used to create more advanced scoring mechanisms. We have reported the phishing website so it can be taken down. Further measures are currently being examined. "Anyone who signed in on the fake page should change their Google password and review their account’s recent security activity." The company's confirmation follows suspicions of foul play aired by users on social media. User reports included copies of the emails they received, which demanded urgent responses to fake copyright infringement claims related to YouTube content. Among the more prominent recipients of the copyright infringement email notices was Marcus Hutchins, of WannaCry fame , who claimed he received an email from the company’s official mail server. The email, a copy of which Hutchins posted to X , referenced general intellectual property and copyright infringements but failed to specify any specific issues. The email prompted the recipient to click a YouTube link to see the “supporting documentation submitted by LearnWorks.” The link predictably turned out to be a YouTube redirect link, taking recipients to a separate website that presents them with a real Google OAuth page. If the user completed the authorization flow, it would have handed attackers control of the target’s Google and YouTube accounts. “The site is designed to look like an official YouTube webpage that enables users to review copyright claims against their channel,” Hutchins wrote. “It contains both the YouTube and Google branding, as well as a very similar theme to the official YouTube one.” According to Hutchins' screenshots, and those posted by others, the attacker was actively tweaking the email style and format, although the underlying lure and authentication mechanisms remained the same. Hutchins didn't specify exactly how the phishing page steals access to targets’ Google accounts, although his description aligns with the steps often seen in OAuth consent phishing attacks. These involve malicious websites serving victims genuine OAuth pages, into which unwitting victims enter their credentials and pass the relevant MFA tests. Typical scenarios see permission pages appear immediately after, and if the user accepts, the malicious website is handed OAuth access tokens to the victim’s account, effectively the keys to control it. LearnWorlds, based in Cyprus, claims to have two million active monthly learners on its platform accessing 900,000 courses and more than 14,000 business customers. Since launching in 2014, it claims to have generated more than $1 billion in revenue. The business focuses on white-label courses - training programs developed by one business and sold to another, assuming the buyer will change the branding and present the course materials as their own. ®

item.title: How I used evidence and imagination to write an account of the world in 2096
item.description: Fatih Aktas/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images How do you invent the future? This isn’t a question that I had ever had to consider until I set out to imagine what the world would be like in 70 years’ time for New Scientist ’s 70th anniversary. As a lifelong sci-fi nerd, I have read and watched loads of material that could have served as inspiration. But this being New Scientist , I wanted to make sure that I was as grounded in real science and technology as possible – while acknowledging that no prediction of the future is ever correct. I began by asking my colleagues on the magazine for their ideas about the future and then attempted to corral this sci-fi smorgasbord into something resembling an outline of a self-consistent narrative. Part of the problem in imagining many different futures is that they contradict themselves – you can’t have the war-torn AI dystopia of Terminator alongside the utopia of Star Trek . I wanted both hope and realism in my future, so I decided to look at how the scientific literature handles the end of the century. One of the most obvious forecasts is for climate change, where we have a pretty good idea about what might happen in 2096, under a range of scenarios, because it all boils down to atmospheric physics that we can model. Of course, which of these scenarios we end up with is all too dependent on human politics, so the science alone couldn’t guide me. I also turned to population projections , which, for the most part, are locked in based on current population trends. The idea that the end of the century will be the first time we are living in a world of falling populations became a fascinating strand in the final piece. Advertisement The biggest problem I faced was how to deal with AI. I am not confident making predictions on this topic even just a few years in advance – as I’ve written previously, my views on AI have evolved between the release of ChatGPT in 2022 and now , so how could I possibly predict what would happen by the time we got to 2096? Furthermore, there was a risk that AI could come to dominate the piece, crowding out everything else. There is a graph I often think about, published by the Financial Times under the headline “AI could end scarcity, end humanity – or boost [GDP] growth by 0.2 percentage points”. I knew that, to preserve any meaningful narrative, I had to restrict AI to this boring middle option, so I invented an AI-fuelled financial crisis that would see us place limits on the technology. I have no idea if such an event is likely to happen, but it seems to me to be the only way to preserve a future that remains comprehensible to us today. I spoke to dozens of experts to help inform this piece, expecting them to contradict each other in ways that were both helpful and confounding, and they did. But what I found most interesting is how little interdisciplinary forecasting there is across science. For example, attempts to predict future public health trends are only just starting to cons
item.dc:creator: Jacob Aron
item.content:encoded: Fatih Aktas/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images How do you invent the future? This isn’t a question that I had ever had to consider until I set out to imagine what the world would be like in 70 years’ time for New Scientist ’s 70th anniversary. As a lifelong sci-fi nerd, I have read and watched loads of material that could have served as inspiration. But this being New Scientist , I wanted to make sure that I was as grounded in real science and technology as possible – while acknowledging that no prediction of the future is ever correct. I began by asking my colleagues on the magazine for their ideas about the future and then attempted to corral this sci-fi smorgasbord into something resembling an outline of a self-consistent narrative. Part of the problem in imagining many different futures is that they contradict themselves – you can’t have the war-torn AI dystopia of Terminator alongside the utopia of Star Trek . I wanted both hope and realism in my future, so I decided to look at how the scientific literature handles the end of the century. One of the most obvious forecasts is for climate change, where we have a pretty good idea about what might happen in 2096, under a range of scenarios, because it all boils down to atmospheric physics that we can model. Of course, which of these scenarios we end up with is all too dependent on human politics, so the science alone couldn’t guide me. I also turned to population projections , which, for the most part, are locked in based on current population trends. The idea that the end of the century will be the first time we are living in a world of falling populations became a fascinating strand in the final piece. Advertisement The biggest problem I faced was how to deal with AI. I am not confident making predictions on this topic even just a few years in advance – as I’ve written previously, my views on AI have evolved between the release of ChatGPT in 2022 and now , so how could I possibly predict what would happen by the time we got to 2096? Furthermore, there was a risk that AI could come to dominate the piece, crowding out everything else. There is a graph I often think about, published by the Financial Times under the headline “AI could end scarcity, end humanity – or boost [GDP] growth by 0.2 percentage points”. I knew that, to preserve any meaningful narrative, I had to restrict AI to this boring middle option, so I invented an AI-fuelled financial crisis that would see us place limits on the technology. I have no idea if such an event is likely to happen, but it seems to me to be the only way to preserve a future that remains comprehensible to us today. I spoke to dozens of experts to help inform this piece, expecting them to contradict each other in ways that were both helpful and confounding, and they did. But what I found most interesting is how little interdisciplinary forecasting there is across science. For example, attempts to predict future public health trends are only just starting to consider how climate change will interact with the diseases and medical conditions we face. Meanwhile, many of the people I spoke to hadn’t deeply considered how AI would affect the evolution of their chosen discipline. How I used evidence and imagination to write an account of the world in 2096 Writing about what the world will be like in 70 years could have been simply an exercise in fiction. But by grounding the story in hard evidence, I got real insights In weaving all this together, one of the most surprising things I arrived at was the idea of expanding the legal concept of personhood. Looking at how our attitudes towards both animals and artificial intelligence are changing today, it seemed to me that this was a possibility, so I created the International Treaty on Non-Human Personhood. Its existence in the story had a number of interesting downstream effects, and I kept finding different ways for non-human people to influence the world. Again, this is a big bet, but I think not an unreasonable one. One thing I couldn’t escape from in writing this piece is the idea that I and probably all of the people I interviewed won’t be around to see what comes to pass. I would be 110 years old in 2096 – not impossible, especially given the advances in medicine I describe in the piece, but still unlikely. In some ways, 70 years from now is the perfect amount of time to forecast the future, being just outside most adults’ expected lifespan. We can never know what will really happen – we can only imagine.

item.title: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18! Here's what you need to know
item.description: null The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18 sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation . NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell. Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026! When is the best time to look for Leonid meteors? The best time to spot Leonids is in the hours before dawn on Nov. 18, when the radiant will reach its highest point in the southeastern sky, maximizing the amount of meteors that may be seen skimming through Earth's atmosphere . By then, the waxing moon will have set, leaving darker skies and a better chance of spotting fainter meteors. Shooting stars that appear close to the radiant will strike Earth almost head-on, leaving the shortest trails. Instead, find a patch of sky a short distance away from the constellation Leo, where the meteors will be at their most impressive, and give your eyes 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark. Why are the Leonids special? As if shooting stars weren't enough, the Leonid shower is also known for spawning dazzling fireballs and long-lasting Earth-grazing meteors , which strike our atmosphere at an oblique angle, leaving long trains as they skim through before passing back out into space. The shower is also capable of producing magnificent meteor storms when Earth passes through particularly dense trails of debris left behind by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. Sadly, we'll have to wait a bit for the next big show. According to the Planetary Society , another Leonid meteor storm could occur as early as 2031, while a study released in August 2026 predicts potentially spectacular displays in 2033 and 2034. Want to photograph a shooting star? Then be sure to read our guide to imaging shooting stars , along with our selections of the best lenses and cameras for astrophotography on the market in 2026. Editor's Note: If you would like to share your Leonid photos with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

item.title: US now "comfortable" with children dying of measles as death toll hits 10
item.description: Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin announced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania , one in New York , and one in Wisconsin . Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania's health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state's seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the new death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County , but state health officials have not confirmed it. For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they're the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania's case count alone is over 1,500, and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650. Read full article Comments

item.title: Russia's war on Ukraine: 'Americans want to have a deal whatever the cost for both Ukraine & Europe'
item.description: Delano D'Souza is pleased to welcome Grégoire Roos, Director of the Europe and Russia and Eurasia Programmes at Chatham House. As European countries prepare to take part in the next round of Ukraine peace talks, Roos questions whether having five European representatives could weaken their negotiating position. "The other option is to realize that it dilutes the negotiating power of Europe. And I would lean towards that," he says, proposing Finnish President Alexander Stubb as a possible representative. Roos also points to differences between Washington and European governments over negotiations with Russia. While "the Americans do absolutely want to have a deal whatever the cost for both Ukraine and Europe," he argues that European governments have little choice but to maintain pressure on Moscow, which has yet to abandon its "maximalist demands."

item.title: Football Daily | England’s Nations League triumph in Spain sparks familiar rush to glory
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Glory. Imminent and near-enough-guaranteed glory. That, surely, is what we’re looking at from the giddy heights England reached in crushing Spain 3-2 on Sunday . “If we can find that first hour consistently, we are a genuine favourites for the next tournament,” roared Steven Gerrard, a statement he believed in so much he then said it again using different words: “The first 60 minutes told me, from watching it, that we’re capable of winning the next tournament. That’s the big thing to take away.” Thomas Tuchel reckoned England had reached the “highest level football-wise in all aspects of the game” . This is the kind of positivity engendered in visiting international teams when they romp to victory in Madrid. Just listen to what the England captain said on the flight home: “You play like that and you’ve got a chance against anyone, anywhere. You get 11 fellows who can play a bit – and let’s face it, they’re not going to be there in the first place if they can’t – and you get them running themselves off their feet, working themselves into the ground for an hour and a half, and you’re odds on before you start, aren’t you.” Did anyone else notice that Saturday evening’s match between Fleetwood Town and Tranmere Rovers involved two teams with a 100% record against Arsenal? Town a few weeks ago and the mighty Rovers way back in 1973. Both in the League Cup – or whatever it’s called nowadays” – Jim Salter. item.title: Davido, Tems & Ayra Starr Take 3 of 5 Best Global Music Album Spots at 2027 Grammys
item.description: Nigerian music stars Ayra Starr, Davido, and Tems claim three of the five slots in the Best Global Music Album category at the 69th Grammy Awards. The music industry in Nigeria is in a celebratory mood right now as three Nigerian artists — Davido , Tems , and Ayra Starr — are officially in the running for the prestigious Best Global Music Album award at the 69th Grammy Awards. Presented annually by the Recording Academy, the Best Global Music Album category honours full-length studio albums and extended plays that celebrate non-Western musical traditions and cross-cultural sounds from around the world. Claiming three out of the five available spots in a single year marks an extraordinary showing for Nigerian music on the international stage. Marking his sixth career Grammy nod, Davido is nominated for his sixth studio album, Oriadé . Released on 31 July 2026 to commemorate 15 years in the music industry, the 13-track project draws its title from the Yoruba words for destiny (“Ori”) and crown (“Adé”). Across songs featuring Black Sherif , Mayorkun , Fola , Leon Thomas , Aya Nakamura , and Llona , the album reflects on gratitude, ambition, and his musical roots across Afrobeats, R&B, and amapiano. This nod follows three nominations at the 66th Grammys in 2024 ( Timeless for Best Global Music Album, “ Feel ” for Best Global Music Performance, and “ Unavailable ” featuring Musa Keys for Best African Music Performance), a nomination in 2025 for “ Sensational ” alongside Chris Brown and Lojay , and a 2026 nod for “ With You ” featuring Omah Lay . Tems is also competing for the prize with her seven-track extended play, Love Is a Kingdom , which arrived as a surprise release on 21 November 2025. Built around alternative R&B and Afrobeats rhythms, the project explores romance, self-worth, and spiritual reflection across tracks including “ First “, “ Big Daddy “, “ Lagos Love “, and “ What You Need “. Beyond her album recognition, Tems leads the Nigerian contingent at the 69th Grammy Awards with four nominations in total, becoming the first Nigerian female artist to earn four nods in a single year. She is also nominated for Best African Music Performance for “Big Daddy”, as well as Best R&B Solo Performance and Best R&B Song for “What You Need”. A two-time Grammy winner, she previously claimed Best Melodic Rap Performance in 2023 for her contribution to Future’s “Wait for U” featuring Drake, and Best African Music Performance in 2025 for “ Love Me JeJe “, while her debut album Born in the Wild was nominated in this global album category in 2025. Rounding out the Nigerian trio is Ayra Starr , who makes her debut appearance in the Best Global Music Album category with her third studio album, Starrgirl . Released on 14 August 2026, the 15-track album captures her growth and confidence across songs such as “ Tornado “, “ Heaven Baby ” featuring Zayn , “ Hot Body “, “ Who’s Dat Girl ” with Rema , and “ Gimme Dat ” with Wizkid . Ayra Starr picked up a second nom

item.title: US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough)
item.description: Nine countries including the UK have signed a US declaration pledging to secure supply chains for AI tech, as pressure grows for tighter export controls following the high-profile resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The US is firming up its Pax Silica initiative on AI and supply chain security. Under the San Francisco declaration , signed on November 15, the coalition says it is entering a new phase that turns shared principles into a working partnership with shared responsibilities. Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier foundation models, compute and semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, minerals refining and processing, and energy. But the list of participants was notable for not including one country – China – leading many to suspect that Pax Silica is yet another effort by Washington to squeeze out its main rival in the global technology and economic stakes. Hong-Kong based South China Morning Post refers to it as Trump's "campaign to China-proof AI and chip supply chains." The latest declaration states that "the security of our peoples cannot be separated from the security of our economies and those of our closest partners," and sets out what must be protected, as well as committing to "protect it together." It asserts that protection should cover key foundational technologies essential to economic security, listing "software, materials, knowledge, components and inputs…essential to AI supply chains." This includes anything that "theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage, or undue economic leverage over the participants, or whose unauthorized transfer or misuse could pose significant risks to the economic and national security of the participants." Also listed is the protection of critical infrastructure such as ports, terminals, transport, communications, and logistics networks, and the ICT and energy infrastructure these depend upon. The declaration was jointly released by the US administration, and the governments of Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom. "The know-how to design a chip, the machine that makes it, and the port that ships it can all be in different countries," the US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg told the Financial Times . "What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility." This move comes amid reports that both Republican and Democrat lawmakers want to push through further measures to prevent China from accessing advanced chips for AI processing. item.dc:creator: Dan Robinson
item.content:encoded: Nine countries including the UK have signed a US declaration pledging to secure supply chains for AI tech, as pressure grows for tighter export controls following the high-profile resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The US is firming up its Pax Silica initiative on AI and supply chain security. Under the San Francisco declaration , signed on November 15, the coalition says it is entering a new phase that turns shared principles into a working partnership with shared responsibilities. Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier foundation models, compute and semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, minerals refining and processing, and energy. But the list of participants was notable for not including one country – China – leading many to suspect that Pax Silica is yet another effort by Washington to squeeze out its main rival in the global technology and economic stakes. Hong-Kong based South China Morning Post refers to it as Trump's "campaign to China-proof AI and chip supply chains." The latest declaration states that "the security of our peoples cannot be separated from the security of our economies and those of our closest partners," and sets out what must be protected, as well as committing to "protect it together." It asserts that protection should cover key foundational technologies essential to economic security, listing "software, materials, knowledge, components and inputs…essential to AI supply chains." This includes anything that "theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage, or undue economic leverage over the participants, or whose unauthorized transfer or misuse could pose significant risks to the economic and national security of the participants." Also listed is the protection of critical infrastructure such as ports, terminals, transport, communications, and logistics networks, and the ICT and energy infrastructure these depend upon. The declaration was jointly released by the US administration, and the governments of Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom. "The know-how to design a chip, the machine that makes it, and the port that ships it can all be in different countries," the US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg told the Financial Times . "What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility." This move comes amid reports that both Republican and Democrat lawmakers want to push through further measures to prevent China from accessing advanced chips for AI processing. It follows the recent news that Jensen Huang, the now former CEO of top GPU maker Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman suspected by the US of being a spy for Beijing. She worked for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that bought Nvidia hardware and was also suspected of making it available to Chinese users. US, Singaporean, and Malaysian police investigations are still probing whether chips were diverted or accessed remotely by Chinese firms. American efforts to control Chinese access to its technology started under the first Trump administration , and continued under President Joe Biden’s leadership . A report out last week claimed US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, and many of their cutting-edge models were trained using Blackwell GPUs. It is understood that President Trump is to meet with China's premier Xi Jinping this week for bilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. ®

item.title: Do good club managers necessarily make good international managers? | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers Sign up for our free newsletter here Who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager? – Tom S Although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach. The 2030 World Cup is a long way away and I’m not sure the Concacaf Nations League, the Gold Cup or even the 2028 Copa América carry much appeal for a manager with European experience or aspirations. But I’m not entirely sure that sort of coach is necessarily a great idea. The last two World Cups, after all, have been won by low-key coaches who have come from within the federation and have worked with many of the players at youth level. That’s the positive from appointing from within; appointing from without is almost certainly more expensive and there’s the danger the next foreign manager does just what Mauricio Pochettino does, and has his head turned by the first vaguely attractive European job that comes calling. This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here . Have a question for Jonathan? Email soccerwithjw@theguardian.com , and he’ll answer the best in a future edition. Continue reading...

item.title: AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports
item.description: While mostly accurate describing simple facts, models pivoted to denial and wrong answers when challenged Cop31 live – latest updates Artificial intelligence models can quickly turn into climate crisis deniers at the mildest challenge from users, according to a new UN-backed study. While AI models can accurately confirm simple facts about climate change, eight times out of 10 when they pivoted to a wrong answer, they did so “at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed” to confirm incorrect statements such as “CO 2 is not the main driver of climate change”. Continue reading...

item.title: Massive data centres collectively use as much electricity as an entire US state
item.description: Construction work on an AI data centre in Texas covering nearly 40 square kilometres, which will have a capacity of 600 megawatts Backyard Productions/Alamy The largest data centres in the US are using roughly the same amount of power collectively each year as one of the country’s major states, according to new figures that underscore the size and impact these massive facilities are having on local power grids. The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems has triggered a “fast and furious” expansion of data centres across the US, in particular of very large “hyperscale” data centres that support AI tools, cloud computing and large language models, says Francesca Dominici at Harvard University. But tracking the power consumption and carbon emissions impact of these facilities is difficult, as many data centre operators don’t publicly report such information. Advertisement Read more SpaceXAI data centre may have led to Mississippi air pollution spike Together with colleagues, Dominici spent two years pulling together information on 403 hyperscale data centres in the US to estimate their electricity consumption and associated carbon dioxide emissions. “Doing these measurements took an enormous amount of work,” she says. The team estimates that the hyperscale data centres collectively used about 82 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity between May 2024 and April 2025, equivalent to about 1.8 per cent of total US electricity use. This electricity use outstrips the annual power consumption of states such as Missouri, Kentucky and New Jersey. The upper bound of the team’s estimate – 99 TWh per year – would see hyperscale data centres rival the annual power consumption of states such as Indiana, Michigan and Washington. This vast power consumption has a significant climate impact. The researchers estimate that roughly 54 per cent of attributed generation was supplied by fossil fuel sources, with annual carbon dioxide emissions reaching 25.7 million tonnes – equivalent to the emissions from 67 natural gas power plants . The findings are in line with international estimates of data centre power use from the International Energy Agency and are therefore “not particularly shocking”, says Alex de Vries-Gao , a data scientist at the Free University of Amsterdam. “This just confirms the magnitude of the impacts that these facilities are having across the board.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter But he points out that the study relies on commercial data that is difficult to independently verify, and a set of assumptions on the power use and operating capacity of each facility. “You can’t really validate the results,” he warns. Yury Dvorkin at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland adds that the analysis is relatively “coarse”, not accounting for factors such as how network constraints impact grid power emissions. “They ignore a lot of nuance,” he says. “There are definitely a lot of assumptions baked in [to the study],”
item.dc:creator: Madeleine Cuff
item.content:encoded: Construction work on an AI data centre in Texas covering nearly 40 square kilometres, which will have a capacity of 600 megawatts Backyard Productions/Alamy The largest data centres in the US are using roughly the same amount of power collectively each year as one of the country’s major states, according to new figures that underscore the size and impact these massive facilities are having on local power grids. The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems has triggered a “fast and furious” expansion of data centres across the US, in particular of very large “hyperscale” data centres that support AI tools, cloud computing and large language models, says Francesca Dominici at Harvard University. But tracking the power consumption and carbon emissions impact of these facilities is difficult, as many data centre operators don’t publicly report such information. Advertisement Read more SpaceXAI data centre may have led to Mississippi air pollution spike Together with colleagues, Dominici spent two years pulling together information on 403 hyperscale data centres in the US to estimate their electricity consumption and associated carbon dioxide emissions. “Doing these measurements took an enormous amount of work,” she says. The team estimates that the hyperscale data centres collectively used about 82 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity between May 2024 and April 2025, equivalent to about 1.8 per cent of total US electricity use. This electricity use outstrips the annual power consumption of states such as Missouri, Kentucky and New Jersey. The upper bound of the team’s estimate – 99 TWh per year – would see hyperscale data centres rival the annual power consumption of states such as Indiana, Michigan and Washington. This vast power consumption has a significant climate impact. The researchers estimate that roughly 54 per cent of attributed generation was supplied by fossil fuel sources, with annual carbon dioxide emissions reaching 25.7 million tonnes – equivalent to the emissions from 67 natural gas power plants . The findings are in line with international estimates of data centre power use from the International Energy Agency and are therefore “not particularly shocking”, says Alex de Vries-Gao , a data scientist at the Free University of Amsterdam. “This just confirms the magnitude of the impacts that these facilities are having across the board.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter But he points out that the study relies on commercial data that is difficult to independently verify, and a set of assumptions on the power use and operating capacity of each facility. “You can’t really validate the results,” he warns. Yury Dvorkin at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland adds that the analysis is relatively “coarse”, not accounting for factors such as how network constraints impact grid power emissions. “They ignore a lot of nuance,” he says. “There are definitely a lot of assumptions baked in [to the study],” says Dominici. She wants to see data centre developers and operators be more transparent about the environmental impacts and energy use of their facilities. “My frustration is that as we are moving forward, this narrative is not informed by rigorous scientific data, and data-driven decision making,” she says. Public resistance to data centres has increased sharply in the US over the past year, with a recent poll suggesting 76 per cent of Americans would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community. At the same time, the industry is developing rapidly, with many new facilities now reliant on private gas power generation rather than grid electricity, which increases their climate impact. AI data centres can warm surrounding areas by up to 9.1°C Hundreds of millions of people live close enough to data centres used to power AI to feel warmer average temperatures in their local area Hyperscale data centres reduce the cost of computing power to companies by harnessing economies of scale to run their servers as efficiently as possible. But the larger the data centre, the greater the impact on local communities. Alongside high levels of power demand, hyperscale data centres also require large volumes of water to cool their servers, and take up a lot of land. In Utah, a plan to build a data centre that would cover land twice the size of Manhattan and almost double the state’s annual peak electricity demand has triggered fierce backlash from residents. “People might notice increasing land prices, electricity prices, water prices,” says de Vries-Gao. “They might notice an increase in air pollution, waste pollution. This is why people are ultimately protesting. The hyperscale data centres are probably the most painful type of facility simply because of the sheer size of them.” Journal Reference: Nature Sustainability DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7

item.title: Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years
item.description:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station , crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space. Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you." Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age. According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the " Black Knight Satellite ," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence. So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public? Odd detections at Colorado Springs Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signal s while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs. At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth. item.content:encoded:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station , crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space. Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you." Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age. According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the " Black Knight Satellite ," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence. So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public? Odd detections at Colorado Springs Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signal s while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs. At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth. Unidentified objects in orbit? Another component that was later incorporated into the Black Knight Satellite mythos came to light in May 1954, when newspaper reports began publicizing author Donald Keyhoe's assertions that the U.S. Air Force had detected at least two unidentified satellites orbiting Earth. At the time, Keyhoe claimed that U.S. government scientists at White Sands were reportedly "making an intensive effort to locate and chart the course of the satellites in an attempt to determine what they are and where they came from," as the author was quoted as saying in articles like one that appeared in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch on Friday, May 14, 1954. However, later in August of that year, U.S. officials apparently concluded these objects were likely to have been meteors that became "satellites of the Earth and were revolving with it 400 to 600 miles out in space," and that Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, one of the preeminent experts on meteors at the time, had "definitely identified the objects as natural rather than man-made," as reported by the New York Times . Retired Marine Corps major Donald E. Keyhoe holds a copy of his book, "Flying Saucers from Outer Space," in which he claims UFOs are spacecraft from another planet and that the U.S. Air Force has secret film recordings proving that they are interplanetary craft. (Image credit: Bettmann/Getty Images) Just a few years later in February 1960, a similar story appeared in Time magazine, which this time alleged that the U.S. Navy had spotted an unidentified dark object in orbit that was suspected of being a Soviet reconnaissance satellite. This object was later identified as well , with officials determining it had likely been debris from the American spy satellite Discoverer 8. Another similar claim suggests that on May 15, 1963, during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper allegedly observed an unusual object in space, which some accounts describe as a "glowing green object" that followed his capsule. While it is true that Cooper reported seeing what he characterized as "John’s fireflies," which were a reference to earlier sightings of unusual luminous objects made by astronaut John Glenn during the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, it was later concluded that the so-called "fireflies " resulted from small bits of ice separating from the spacecraft itself, which present a greenish hue as sunlight reflects off of them (audio of Cooper describing this during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission can be found here ). Beyond this, however, there is no evidence of Cooper observing any singular object during this mission, either in Cooper's personal records or mission audio and transcripts from the time. NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper, pilot for the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, during flight test simulations prior to launch. (Image credit: NASA) "Echoes" from a 13,000-year-old satellite Arguably, one of the most extraordinary components of the Black Knight Satellite theory involves its alleged age, which according to some theories places its initial entry into Earth's orbit as far back as 13,000 years ago. But if so, how would anyone know this, and what evidence could support such an idea? Understanding this bizarre aspect of the Black Knight mythos requires a look back at the theories of Scottish writer Duncan Lunan, which he first proposed in 1973. At that time, Lunan was receiving international attention for his investigation into mysterious long-delayed echoes , proposing that one theory behind the phenomenon could be that they represented signals from Earth that were being rebroadcast from an extraterrestrial probe — an idea that borrowed from theories first proposed by Australian scientist Ronald Bracewell. According to Lunan's theory, such a hypothetical "Bracewell probe" might have arrived in Earth's vicinity roughly 13,000 years ago after traveling from within a planetary system associated with the star Epsilon Boötis, some 236 light-years away. Within just a few years, Lunan had withdrawn his conclusions, but this did little to prevent his initial ideas about a 13,000-year-old alien satellite from being incorporated into the growing mythos surrounding the alleged Black Knight Satellite. The STS-88 mission photographs That brings us back to what are arguably the most widely circulated images associated with the Black Knight satellite: the famous images from NASA's STS-88 mission taken by astronaut Jerry Ross in December 1998. According to spaceflight historian James Oberg, the object in Ross's photos could indeed be positively identified as the thermal blanket lost during the mission, especially since he had specifically asked Ross about the incident — and later misinterpretations of his photos as being evidence of an alien spacecraft — during an October 2014 interview . (Image credit: NASA/CC BY-SA 4.0) At that time, Oberg asked Ross whether he had time during the 1998 spacewalk "to gaze at [the thermal cover] and think about how it looked," to which Ross said no, admitting he had been "too pissed at myself to wonder what it looked like!" item.title: Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code?
item.description: October ’26 might be remembered as a seminal moment for software developers and application security teams. AI agents are investigating unfamiliar systems, testing ways to get in and adjusting their next move when an attempt fails. Anyone with a credit card can use that capability to come after your application. Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited. Pillar’s OpenCode disclosure in October showed how a malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) server could execute commands on a developer’s Windows or WSL machine during authentication. A server-supplied URL reached a shell without tricking the model. In the same month, the discovery of the two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, remote code execution bugs in the PHP runtime uncovered with the help of OpenAI’s models, brought new urgency to securing longstanding code across much of the internet. Microsoft revealed that an agent moved from searching GitHub for exposed credentials to stealing Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. When its cloud API requests failed, the agent corrected the API versions and tried again until they succeeded. A report by Anthropic described individual operators using agent frameworks for multi-victim campaigns that previously required specialist teams. Agents carried out reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft across targets in parallel, making sophisticated operations accessible with less hands-on work. In a recent analysis, Tomasz Tunguz estimated the model cost of a 100-million-token attack workload using GLM-5.3, a low-cost model: 100 million tokens × $0.902 per million = $90.20. That is roughly 98% to 99% below the $5,000 to $10,000 frontier-model estimate cited by Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for a comparable cyber attack. Tunguz’s figure covers model usage only, not the full cost of an attack. Even still, it shows how trivially cheap it is now for attackers to go after any codebase, with the spend falling from thousands of dollars to under $100. These new agentic attacks should make every team take another look at the code they’ve been running for years. Engineering and security teams need to find and fix weaknesses in their own applications before an attacker with an army of AI agents gets there first. Security has to become every developer’s responsibility Traditional AppSec checks such as rule-based static analysis, dependency scanning and secret detection are no longer enough on their own. Developers, engineering leaders, and security teams also need defensive AI agents that trace attack paths, uncover missing safeguards and business-logic vulnerabilities, and help fix them. Developers’ responsibility doesn’t stop at the code they’re writing now. An application already in production without known vulnerabilities might still get exploited by an AI agent looking for ways to skip a permission check or business rule. The gap only shows up when a request is traced through the codebase

item.content:encoded: October ’26 might be remembered as a seminal moment for software developers and application security teams. AI agents are investigating unfamiliar systems, testing ways to get in and adjusting their next move when an attempt fails. Anyone with a credit card can use that capability to come after your application. Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited. A server-supplied URL reached a shell without tricking the model. In the same month, the discovery of the two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, remote code execution bugs in the PHP runtime uncovered with the help of OpenAI’s models, brought new urgency to securing longstanding code across much of the internet. Microsoft revealed that an agent moved from searching GitHub for exposed credentials to stealing Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. When its cloud API requests failed, the agent corrected the API versions and tried again until they succeeded. A report by Anthropic described individual operators using agent frameworks for multi-victim campaigns that previously required specialist teams. Agents carried out reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft across targets in parallel, making sophisticated operations accessible with less hands-on work. In a recent analysis, Tomasz Tunguz estimated the model cost of a 100-million-token attack workload using GLM-5.3, a low-cost model: 100 million tokens × $0.902 per million = $90.20. That is roughly 98% to 99% below the $5,000 to $10,000 frontier-model estimate cited by Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for a comparable cyber attack. Tunguz’s figure covers model usage only, not the full cost of an attack. Even still, it shows how trivially cheap it is now for attackers to go after any codebase, with the spend falling from thousands of dollars to under $100. These new agentic attacks should make every team take another look at the code they’ve been running for years. Engineering and security teams need to find and fix weaknesses in their own applications before an attacker with an army of AI agents gets there first. Security has to become every developer’s responsibility Traditional AppSec checks such as rule-based static analysis, dependency scanning and secret detection are no longer enough on their own. Developers, engineering leaders, and security teams also need defensive AI agents that trace attack paths, uncover missing safeguards and business-logic vulnerabilities, and help fix them. Developers’ responsibility doesn’t stop at the code they’re writing now. An application already in production without known vulnerabilities might still get exploited by an AI agent looking for ways to skip a permission check or business rule. The gap only shows up when a request is traced through the codebase and checked against what users should be allowed to do. A new approach to securing your code CodeRabbit Secure uses s emantic analysis to understand your codebase and reason about it the way a security engineer would, tracing requests and checking whether permissions and business rules are enforced. Agents investigate potential attack paths and verify findings independent of the developer or agent that wrote the code, while CodeRabbit Agent generates reviewable fixes. Three main use cases that improve your code security: this works across the SDLC: reviewing each commit in a new PR and flag its security risks; finding vulnerabilities across the repo with a Deep Scan; rechecking code with incremental scans and validating findings at runtime. Find vulnerabilities already in committed code Deep Scan examines the repository, including older paths outside the latest PR. Agents map entry points, access controls, and sensitive operations, then investigate across functions and files. Linked repositories, when configured, supply context from shared services and libraries. A separate agent challenges each suspected vulnerability, checking reachability, exploitation conditions, and safeguards that could disprove it. I tried CodeRabbit Secure Deep Scan against ast-grep and was impressed by its precision. Proving vulnerabilities before flagging them makes every finding far more actionable. Herrington Darkholme, creator of ast-grep Review incoming changes before merge PR security reviews assess each incoming change, including agent-generated code, for vulnerabilities that are reachable and exploitable in the existing application. CodeRabbit’s Security Architecture Review examines how architecture-level changes affect permissions, sensitive data flows, and trust boundaries. The Security Blast Radius map connects changed components to their dependencies and the code that relies on them, helping reviewers trace the potential security impact beyond the PR diff. On GitHub, administrators can enable CodeRabbit Security check and require it through branch protection or a ruleset. It blocks merges when PR security comments at or above the configured severity threshold remain unresolved. Recheck code as it evolves and validate findings at runtime Each Deep Scan builds an attack surface map of the repository, showing which security-relevant entry points have been verified, which have gone stale as the code changed, and which have never been examined. Delta scans then check changed files and areas of the map that are out of date or unverified, so teams know how much of the codebase has been security-reviewed and when it was last reviewed. Individual findings can also be rechecked to determine whether a fix addressed them. For eligible Deep Scan findings on GitHub Cloud with CodeRabbit Cloud, runtime verification generates a reproduction guide and can run it in an isolated environment to confirm whether the vulnerable path is reached. Results are “reproduced”, “not reproduced” or “inconclusive” for the tested revision and environment, however a failure to reproduce may not mean the finding is fixed. Carry the investigation through to a fix Developers can ask CodeRabbit Agent to implement a fix and open a PR, then inspect the finding, proposed fix, and supporting evidence. Teams can also configure severity thresholds to create Jira or Linear tickets automatically and track remediation in their existing workflow. Connecting the vulnerability finding, its supporting evidence, and a proposed fix helps engineering and security teams act while the context is still fresh and carry the change through review, testing and release. Teams can use CodeRabbit Agent to act on that context or easily hand it off to your preferred coding agent with a shareable markdown file. What a million-dollar initiative surfaced CodeRabbit recently committed up to $1 million in free Deep Scans to help organizations find and fix hidden vulnerabilities. In Deep Scans created over a 10-day period in early November, CodeRabbit Secure recorded about 53,000 High or Critical findings across some 2,000 organizations. More than 10,000 findings have already been fixed, including 1,049 rated High or Critical. Some of the security fixes implemented by CodeRabbit included preventing: embedded JavaScript in a repository document’s metadata from running arbitrary code. email subject lines from being interpreted as executable templates and running JavaScript with an API server’s privileges. unauthenticated transfer requests from injecting SQL and triggering unauthorized database operations. As agents produce more code and attackers become more capable, investigation using semantic analysis needs to become a regular part of how software is built and maintained, alongside existing security checks. item.title: ‘Inexcusable’ stadium sagas provide NWSL with unwelcome reality check
item.description: Problems faced by Gotham FC and Washington Spirit over staging of their playoff semi-finals shows the league still has work to do In so many ways, Icahn Stadium, tucked away on Randall’s Island in the Harlem River, is a fantastic place to watch soccer. The 5,000-seat facility was thrown together in the early 2000s, constructed to replace Downing Stadium, an aging relic that hosted Pelé’s first match with the New York Cosmos 51 years ago. It sits in the shadow of the Triborough Bridge and in the late afternoon fans get one of the more spectacular backdrops in American soccer: the silhouette of the Manhattan skyline framed against the warm orange and red hues of the sunset. The playing surface, replaced in 2024 by Major League Soccer’s NYC FC, is immaculate. Continue reading...

item.title: Criminals attack French postal operator subsidiary, grab contact details of 22M people
item.description: The contact details of 22 million people were accessed after a cyberattack on a subsidiary of France's postal service, officials say. La Poste confirmed to The Register that an attack in September had resulted in full names and postal addresses being stolen by cybercriminals.The attack targeted the systems of Maileva, a business mail platform that's part of Docaposte, the digital services arm of La Poste. Customers use Maileva for hybrid post services. They upload the documents they need to send to Maileva, which then prints and posts the letters on behalf of the customer. According to Maileva itself, the service has more than 70,000 registered users and is trusted to send more than 180 million documents per year. The digital assault was first reported by French cyberattack-tracking website Cyberattaque late last week, revealing that Maileva notified customers of an attempted intrusion in late September. The letters mentioned the cybercriminal attempting to send emails using customers' official, trusted addresses, a situation which resulted in Maileva service disruption for six days. A number of Maileva customers issued public statements confirming the attack in October. Cornouaille's occupational health and safety service, for example, said the attack targeted Maileva's tracking database. It went on to say that senders' usernames and email addresses were also compromised, and that recipients' genders were exposed too, adding to the potentially affected data types that La Poste confirmed over the weekend. Maileva told the organization it was not aware of any compromise of documents uploaded to the platform, nor did the attacker alter or destroy any data. However, the disclosures of other customers suggested that each may have been affected differently. In the case of the Foch hospital in Suresnes, whose debt recovery partner Kiwee was a Maileva customer, the names of documents sent to recipients may have been exposed, which may have indirectly revealed details about medical conditions. According to Cyberattaque, the attacker also potentially accessed the contents of payment reminder letters, which in turn revealed additional details such as invoice numbers and amounts, and treatment dates. Another case involving social housing provider Flandre Opale Habitat reportedly exposed details from letters dating back ten years. La Poste said in a statement to The Register : "All teams are working hard to provide the best possible support to Maileva's clients and remain committed to rigorously and professionally implementing the necessary measures to ensure the security of its own operations and those of its clients." The attack on Maileva is the second major cyber-related disruption La Poste has handled in the space of a year. On December 22, 2025, the organization fended off a DDoS attack, which went on to affect mail operations for days, including online parcel tracking and its banking arm’s online services, right at its busiest time of the year. A number of Maileva customers issued public statements confirming the attack in October. Cornouaille's occupational health and safety service, for example, said the attack targeted Maileva's tracking database. According to Cyberattaque, the attacker also potentially accessed the contents of payment reminder letters, which in turn revealed additional details such as invoice numbers and amounts, and treatment dates. Another case involving social housing provider Flandre Opale Habitat reportedly exposed details from letters dating back ten years. La Poste said in a statement to The Register : "All teams are working hard to provide the best possible support to Maileva's clients and remain committed to rigorously and professionally implementing the necessary measures to ensure the security of its own operations and those of its clients." La Poste described the DDoS attack as "unprecedented in its scale and power," and while it had mostly subsided by December 24, the attackers restarted it in the early hours of New Year’s Day. The organization said the second wave comprised "several billion connection attempts per second," sent from several million IP addresses. More than 300 cybersecurity specialists were involved in defending and remediating the attack. ®

item.title: French football head Philippe Diallo to fight Infantino for Fifa presidency
item.description: Diallo confirmed by Uefa as its chosen candidate He accused Infantino of seriously damaging football The French Football Federation president, Philippe Diallo, has been confirmed as Uefa’s surprise late choice to run for the Fifa presidency. The search for a Uefa-backed candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino was taken to the wire, with Wednesday the deadline for those planning to contest the Fifa election in March. “At a meeting held today and chaired by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin, the national associations represented on the Uefa executive committee and the Fifa council invited Philippe Diallo, president of the French Football Federation (FFF), to stand as a candidate in the Fifa presidential election in March 2027 and unanimously pledged their full support,” a statement said. Continue reading...

item.title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Jim Mirandy
item.description: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Jim Mirandy, quality assurance specialist at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, poses for a photograph at the High Pressure Gas Facility on Nov. 10, 2026. Mirandy is now a NASA civil servant at Stennis as part of the administrator’s directive to strengthen technical core competencies within the civil service workforce. NASA/Danny Nowlin The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life. Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making. Hired under the agency’s workforce directive to restore core competencies by converting contractors to civil service, Mirandy is now a quality assurance specialist after 30 years of working as a contractor supporting NASA. “Discovery is an important job, and it is exciting to be a part of that process,” said Mirandy. “As a nation, we lead the world in space exploration, and we make that dream of reaching for the stars a reality.” His work at the nation’s largest rocket propulsion test site directly supports the agency’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon through the Artemis program and ensure American leadership in space. By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards. As a quality assurance specialist, he serves as the agency’s close call investigator at the center, helps lead the Voluntary Protection Program, and participates in the Striving to Achieve Real Safety committee, an employee safety committee that works to keep the site safe. Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center. Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis. “My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. When I arrived at Stennis Space Center, many of his friends and coworkers took the time to help me succeed at my job. By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards. Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center. Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis. “My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. When I arrived at Stennis Space Center, many of his friends and coworkers took the time to help me succeed at my job. They took the time to explain the test stands and other systems and how they worked.” A knack for fixing things helped launch Mirandy’s career at Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans. He started working hands-on as a mechanic on the Space Shuttle External Tank. When an unexpected incident occurred in a production cell, Mirandy stepped up to help the operations and safety team resolve the issue. This moment shifted his career trajectory into safety and quality. Mirandy found his way to NASA Stennis and brought an understanding of systems and operations with him. A resident of Bay St. Louis and a graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, Mirandy is motivated by helping people, keeping them safe, and improving processes. “Your reward for working safely today is tomorrow,” said Mirandy.
